item.title: “Cunda, just as all unwholesome states tend downward and all wholesome states tend upward. So too, Cunda: the harmless person is higher than the harmful…
item.description:
“Cunda, just as all unwholesome states tend downward and all wholesome states tend upward. So too, Cunda: the harmless person is higher than the harmful person; the person who abstains from killing is higher than the killer; the person who abstains from taking what is not given is higher than the taker of what is not given; the person unsmeared by the world, not clinging to personal views, of easy disposition and equanimity, is higher than the person smeared by the world, clinging to personal views, of difficult disposition and lacking equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 8 – Sallekhasutta

item.title: Then the Blessed One gave progressive instruction to the brahmin Pokkharasādi, namely: talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on the heavens; he explained the…
item.description:
Then the Blessed One gave progressive instruction to the brahmin Pokkharasādi, namely: talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on the heavens; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation. When the Blessed One knew that the brahmin Pokkharasādi’s mind was ready, pliant, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, he then taught the Dhamma that the Buddhas have realized, namely: suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Just as a clean cloth, freed from black stains, would properly absorb dye, so too, right there in that seat, the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose in the brahmin Pokkharasādi: ‘Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.’

From: Dīgha Nikāya 3 – Ambaṭṭhasutta

item.title: Venerable Jatukaṇṇī: “Having heard of the hero, free from desire for sensual pleasures, I have come to ask the desireless one, Who has crossed the…
item.description:
Venerable Jatukaṇṇī:
“Having heard of the hero, free from desire for sensual pleasures,
I have come to ask the desireless one,
Who has crossed the flood,
The one born with the eye —
Speak the path of peace,
Let the Blessed One tell it to me as it is.

Having conquered sensual desires,
The Blessed One lives in the world
Like the sun illuminating the earth with its radiance.
O great wise one, teach me the Dhamma —
I am of little wisdom —
That by knowing it, I might overcome birth and old age.”

The Blessed One replied to Jatukaṇṇī:
“Subdue greed for sensual pleasures,
See renunciation as peace.
Do not hold on to or reject anything in the world.

Dry up what has gone before,
Let there be nothing after —
If you grasp nothing in the middle,
You will live at peace.

For one who has no ‘mine’ at all
In name-and-form, O brahmin,
There are no defilements by which
One would be in death’s power.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 5.12

item.title: “‘Māra, Māra,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is Māra?” - “Form, Rādha, is Māra. Feeling is Māra. Perception is Māra. Formations are Māra.…
item.description:
“‘Māra, Māra,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is Māra?” - “Form, Rādha, is Māra. Feeling is Māra. Perception is Māra. Formations are Māra. Consciousness is Māra. Seeing thus, Rādha, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … with feeling … with perception … with formations … with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.11

item.title: “Monks, these six sense bases — unguarded, unprotected, unguarded, unrestrained — bring suffering. What six? The eye sense base, monks — unguarded, unprotected, unguarded, unrestrained…
item.description:
“Monks, these six sense bases — unguarded, unprotected, unguarded, unrestrained — bring suffering. What six? The eye sense base, monks — unguarded, unprotected, unguarded, unrestrained — brings suffering. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind sense base, monks — unguarded, unprotected, unguarded, unrestrained — brings suffering. These six sense bases, monks — unguarded, unprotected, unguarded, unrestrained — bring suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.94

item.title: “Monks, how does a monk practice the qualities befitting an ascetic? Here, monks, for a monk, when the mind of sensual desire exists, that sensual…
item.description:
“Monks, how does a monk practice the qualities befitting an ascetic? Here, monks, for a monk, when the mind of sensual desire exists, that sensual desire is abandoned; when the mind of ill-will exists, that ill-will is abandoned; when the mind of anger exists, that anger is abandoned; when the mind of hostility … hypocrisy … spite … envy … stinginess … deceit … fraud … obstinacy … impetuosity … conceit … arrogance … vanity … heedlessness exists, that heedlessness is abandoned … Monks, I say that if he practices the qualities befitting an ascetic, he can abandon the defilements that are stains of an ascetic, blemishes of an ascetic, faults of an ascetic, leading to a plane of misery, to a bad destination, to the taking up of an evil realm. He sees himself cleansed of all those evil, unwholesome states and sees himself liberated. Because he sees himself cleansed of all those evil, unwholesome states and sees himself liberated, gladness arises; from gladness, joy; from joy, the body becomes tranquil; from bodily tranquility, he experiences ease; from ease, the mind becomes concentrated. I say that it is because of inner mental concentration that he practices the qualities befitting an ascetic.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 40 – Cūḷa-Assapurasutta
